name: FAN3111ESX
title: FAN3111C, FAN3111E: 1 A one-channel fast low-side MOSFET gate driver, SOT23-5
summary: A one-channel low-side driver for the gate of an N-channel enhancement MOSFET, running from 4.5 V to 18 V and delivering 1.4 A peak (1.1 A sink and 0.9 A source with the output at mid-supply). The FAN3111C has two CMOS inputs, IN+ and IN-, whose thresholds scale with VDD, so it works as a non-inverting or an inverting driver with the other input acting as an enable. The FAN3111E has a single non-inverting input whose thresholds follow a 2 V to 5 V reference applied to its XREF pin, for logic running from a lower rail than the driver. Delays are 15 ns typical and edges about 9 ns rising and 8 ns falling into 470 pF; rated for -40 °C to 125 °C ambient.

circuits.title: Dual-input driver enabled, non-inverting configuration
circuits.description: FAN3111C used as a non-inverting driver: the PWM signal goes to IN+ and IN- is tied to GND, so OUT follows PWM. Lifting IN- high instead would disable it.

circuits.title: Dual-input driver enabled, inverting configuration
circuits.description: FAN3111C used as an inverting driver: the PWM signal goes to IN- and IN+ is tied to VDD, so OUT is the complement of PWM. Pulling IN+ to GND instead would hold OUT low.

circuits.title: PFC boost circuit with distributed drivers for parallel power switches Q1A and Q1B
circuits.description: A boost PFC stage whose switch is two MOSFETs in parallel, each with a FAN3111 of its own beside it. One logic PWM line feeds both drivers' IN+. Each driver has a bypass capacitor across VDD and GND and drives its MOSFET gate through 33 Ω, its ground returning at that MOSFET's source. The rectified AC input is filtered by C1, the boost inductor L1 feeds the common drain node, and D1 charges the bulk capacitor C2 that supplies the downstream converters.
notes: Pin 4 of each FAN3111 (IN- on the FAN3111C, XREF on the FAN3111E) has no connection given for this circuit.

circuits.title: Driver for forward converter low-side switch
circuits.description: A single-switch forward converter. The FAN3111 takes PWM on IN+ and drives the low-side MOSFET's gate through a series resistor; the MOSFET switches the transformer primary from VIN to ground. On the secondary, a rectifier diode and a freewheel diode feed an LC output filter.

circuits.title: Driver for two-transistor forward-converter gate transformer
circuits.description: A two-switch forward converter whose two MOSFETs are driven through a gate transformer. The FAN3111 drives the primary of T2 through a 0.1 µF coupling capacitor CC; the other end of that primary is grounded. One T2 secondary drives the high-side MOSFET Q1 between its gate and source, the other drives the low-side Q2 to ground, and each gate is clamped by a pair of back-to-back zeners. Q1 and Q2 put the power transformer T1 primary across VIN; D1 runs from the Q2 drain to VIN and D2 from ground to the Q1 source. The output is taken from T1's secondary, VSEC.

circuits.title: Quasi-static IOUT/VOUT test circuit
circuits.description: The circuit the quasi-static output current is measured in. A 1 kHz square-wave source drives the input; VDD is held by a 4.7 µF ceramic and a 470 µF aluminium electrolytic, with a further 1 µF ceramic right at the driver. OUT drives a 47 nF load capacitor, and a current probe (LeCroy AP015) on the wire from OUT to the load measures IOUT while VOUT is taken across the load.

operation.text: The CMOS thresholds track VDD. At 12 V the input switches high at about 55 % of VDD and low at about 38 %, a hysteresis of about 17 % of VDD. With good decoupling the inputs accept very slow edges, down to DC, so an RC network between the control signal and IN sets a deliberate delay before OUT changes.

The thresholds track the voltage on XREF, normally between 2 V and 5 V; tying XREF to the supply of the logic that drives IN+ makes the part work with TTL and other logic up to 5 V. The input switches high at about 50 % of VXREF and low at about 30 %, a hysteresis of about 20 % of VXREF.

OUT is high only with IN+ high and IN- low. As a non-inverting driver, PWM goes to IN+ and IN- is grounded; pulling IN- high then disables the driver and holds OUT low whatever IN+ does. As an inverting driver, PWM goes to IN- and IN+ is tied high; pulling IN+ to GND then holds OUT low whatever IN- does. Open inputs default to IN+ low and IN- high, so an unconnected driver keeps OUT low.

While VDD rises from 0 V to about 2 V an internal resistor holds OUT low whatever the inputs are. From about 2 V the internal circuits work and OUT follows the inputs. With the inputs commanding low, OUT stays low through the whole VDD ramp and a ground-referenced N-channel MOSFET stays off. With IN+ tied to VDD and IN- to GND, OUT rises with VDD; because OUT is low at low VDD, that arrangement may not suit a high-side P-channel MOSFET, which would be turned on while VDD is low. On the FAN3111E with IN+ grounded, OUT stays low as XREF ramps from 0 to 3.3 V.

The output stage combines bipolar and MOS transistors. The bipolar devices carry most of the current while OUT is between about one third and two thirds of VDD; the MOS devices take OUT the rest of the way to either rail. The aim is the highest current through the Miller plateau, while the gate-drain capacitance is charged or discharged. Where the MOSFET switches at zero voltage and there is no plateau, as in synchronous rectifiers whose body diode already conducts, the driver still delivers its high peak current.
The edge rate at OUT is set by VDD and the load and has no adjustment. A resistor in series with the gate slows the gate's rise or fall.

A low-ESR, low-ESL high-frequency capacitor, CBYP, goes straight across VDD and GND with the shortest traces, on top of the 10 µF to 47 µF bulk electrolytic usually found on driver and controller bias rails. Ceramics of 0.1 µF to 1 µF or more in X5R or X7R are common choices for their temperature behaviour and pulse current capability. CBYP may be split in two: a larger part sized by the equivalent load capacitance, and a 1 nF to 10 nF part placed nearest the VDD and GND pins for the highest-frequency current.

Input circuits are fast, delays short and output peaks exceed 1 A, so OUT moves in anywhere from under 10 ns to over 100 ns. Signal ground and the logic inputs are routed apart from the output current and its power ground; TTL-level thresholds are the most sensitive to this. A driver sitting close to its MOSFET keeps the high-current traces short: less series inductance for fast switching and a small loop that radiates little into the inputs. The output can be retriggered by noise from its own switching or from other sources, notably on breadboards or with long input, enable or output leads, so every pin is wired short and direct.

At turn-on the gate charge comes from the local CBYP, through the driver into the MOSFET gate and back through ground; resistance and inductance in that loop limit the peak current, and keeping the pulse inside the driver-MOSFET loop stops it reaching the PWM controller's analog circuits. At turn-off the driver returns the gate current straight to the MOSFET source; that loop too is kept small and low in resistance and inductance for fast turn-off.

Switching MOSFETs or IGBTs at high frequency can heat a gate driver considerably, so its dissipation and junction temperature are worked out for the application. The loss is mostly gate charge delivered at the switching frequency, plus the internal current drawn while switching, which the IDD against frequency curves give. The gate-drive power divides among the driver's output resistance, any external series resistor and the MOSFET's internal gate resistance.
